text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's Austrian newspapers:

- The European Union will not support financially the Austrian government's plan to pay Bosnian refugees to return to their home country. About three quarters of the refugees are willing to leave Austria.

- Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger has said passing the Maastricht criteria goes before job security. Higher taxes on profits are planned in the government's next tax reform. Labour costs will not be reduced before Austria becomes a member of European Monetary Union.
- Construction group Bau Holding has taken over a Polish hotel group. The company expects an improvement in this year's results.
- Education Minister Elisabeth Gehrer and Social Affairs MInister Lore Hostasch have agreed to provide additional schooling for all 15-year-olds who do not get an apprenticeship.
- Edlinger announced in parliament that a tax reform would not be presented before the year 2000. He would not promise that people would have to pay less tax afterwards.
- Post & Telekom Austria needs money to restrucure the company ahead of its privatisation and the liberalisation of the market.
- The tourism industry is alarmed as studies show that Austrians are saving money on holidays. Carinthia is the country's main victim.
- GiroCredit's supervisory board president Rene Alfons Haiden expects the bank to merge with Die Erste savings bank after the latter takes over Vienna City council's stake in GiroCredit.
- Post & Telekom Austria executive Johannes Ditz says the planned tariffs reform would bring a price reduction of three billion schillings on telephone bills.
- OECD has praised Austria's austerity measures as they have proved successful.
- PSK would welcome Bawag to take over the government's stake in the postal savings bank. Die Erste and GiroCredit are not favoured as minority shareholders.
- Bank Austria will have to sell its stake in one of its construction businesses so that the European Commission will allow it to take over Creditanstalt.
